note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

mandarin.note: How the characters are read today in Beijing, and in the temples and academies of the mainland and Taiwan — the reading this hall's own pronunciation column already gives.

0.why: The text fed is NOT the hall's character, and this is the one place in the Mandarin set where that was forced. `say -v Ting-Ting "乾"` produces a file byte-identical to 干 gān — the simplified merger, the 'dry' reading, and the wrong word for the Heaven trigram. Context does not fix it: 乾坤 is byte-identical to 干坤, and 乾隆 differs from 前隆, so the engine has no qián reading of this graph at all. Since the synthesiser works from syllable and tone alone, feeding any qián character produces the syllable that was wanted, and 前 was verified byte-identical to 錢, 潛 and 虔 — four independent characters, one waveform. What you hear is exactly the correct qián, second tone.
0.compromise: The audio is generated from a different graph than the one on the page. That is provenance, not distortion: the output waveform is identical to what a correct reading of 乾 would produce, and it was the only route, since the voice's misreading survives every context tried. Chronologically: in Middle Chinese this was a voiced velar initial, roughly gjen, and Cantonese kin4 still shows the velar. Mandarin's tɕʰ- is the result of a palatalisation that only completed around the eighteenth century, so the initial consonant of this trigram's name in Beijing today is younger than the Kangxi dictionary. The Yìjīng's own rhymes are Old Chinese and work in neither modern reading.

1.why: Ting-Ting reads the bare traditional character; the reading was confirmed by producing a file byte-identical to 對 duì, so the engine has both the syllable and the falling fourth tone right.
1.compromise: Correct modern Mandarin, and a thousand years from the text that names it. Middle Chinese had a voiced dental initial here, roughly dwajH; Mandarin devoiced it and reassigned the syllable to the fourth tone, so the [t] you hear is a devoicing, not a survival. The Shuōguà's gloss of 兌 by 說 turns on a phonetic relationship in the ancient language that neither modern reading preserves.

2.why: The bare character, confirmed byte-identical to 梨 lí — same syllable, same rising second tone. Nothing needed forcing here.
2.compromise: One of the least-changed syllables in the hall, but 'least changed' is relative: Middle Chinese lje had a medial glide and a different rime, and the rising tone you hear is a modern reflex of the Middle Chinese level tone in the lower register, not the ancient contour itself. Nobody knows what the pitch of a Zhou-period 離 sounded like, because Old Chinese probably had no tones at all — the tone categories arose later, from lost final consonants.

3.why: The bare character, confirmed byte-identical to 鎮 zhèn. Both syllable and fourth tone are right.
3.compromise: The retroflex [ʈʂ] is a Mandarin development: Middle Chinese had a palatal affricate here (roughly tsyinH), and the retroflex series is a later northern innovation that Cantonese never made. The final -n is genuinely old and survives in both readings. The tone is modern.

4.why: A relatively rare character, so it was worth checking rather than assuming: confirmed byte-identical to 訓 xùn, which settles both the syllable and the tone.
4.compromise: The initial is the clearest single piece of Mandarin youth in this hall. Middle Chinese had a plain [s] here (roughly swonH); the [ɕ] you hear is the product of the palatalisation that swept Mandarin sibilants and velars into one series before front vowels, a change of roughly the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Cantonese seon3 still has the [s]. So the wind trigram's name in Beijing is pronounced with a consonant that did not exist when the Shuōguà was written.

5.why: The bare character, confirmed byte-identical to 砍 kǎn. The slower rate of 140 matters more here than almost anywhere: an isolated third tone is a full 214 dip, and at the default 175 a single syllable can be clipped to a half-third.
5.compromise: The rime is wrong by one feature and it is a feature Mandarin lost across the board: this syllable ended in -m in Middle Chinese (roughly khomX), and Mandarin merged all final -m into -n during the Ming. You are hearing kǎn where the Qieyun had khom. Cantonese ham2 still ends in -m — click it — though Cantonese has itself lenited the initial aspirated velar to [h], so neither reading is whole.

6.why: A rare character; confirmed byte-identical to 亙 gèn, which settles the reading. Some readers know 艮 only as a component and would guess wrongly at it, so the check was worth making.
6.compromise: Segmentally among the more conservative in the set — the velar initial and the -n are both old — but the vowel and the tone are modern Mandarin, and the fourth tone here reflects the Middle Chinese departing-tone category rather than any recoverable ancient pitch. 艮其背 in the fifty-second hexagram is Warring States language; Mandarin is not its sound.

7.why: The bare character, confirmed byte-identical to 昆 kūn. Aspirated velar, labial glide and high level first tone all correct.
7.compromise: Unusually conservative: the aspirated velar survived Mandarin's palatalisation because the following vowel is back, not front, so 坤 kept the [kʰ] that 乾 and 氣 lost. That is an accident of the rime, not a general preservation. The first tone is the modern reflex of the Middle Chinese level tone in the upper register; it is a category that survived, not a contour.

8.why: The bare character, confirmed byte-identical to 到 dào. The single most-clicked sign in the hall, so it was verified first and at both rates.
8.compromise: Middle Chinese had a voiced initial here, roughly dawX in the rising tone; Mandarin devoiced it and moved the syllable into the fourth tone by the regular 濁上變去 shift, so both the consonant and the tone you hear are consequences of that one change. Cantonese dou6 registers the same history differently, in its lower tone register. Neither is the sound of 道可道: the Dàodé jīng's opening pun works in any reading because it is a pun on the graph, but the Odes-era rhymes that the same corpus draws on do not work in Mandarin at all.

9.why: The bare character. Ting-Ting reads it as an ordinary word and it is a monophone with one dictionary reading; the clip is a plain, correct dé.
9.compromise: This is one of five readings in the two systems that could NOT be confirmed by the homophone test, and it should not borrow the others' certainty. No unambiguous dé partner exists: 得 is a polyphone (its isolated reading here is neither dé nor shí, so it proves nothing), and 徳 is a graphic variant of 德 itself, so its byte-identity is circular. The reading is almost certainly right and is stated as such, but it was not verified. Chronologically this is the hall's flagship loss: 德 ended in -k in Middle Chinese, roughly tok, an entering-tone syllable with a hard final stop. Mandarin has deleted the stop and the whole tone category with it, so dé shows no trace of it. Click the Cantonese button and you get dak1, with the -k still there.

10.why: The bare traditional character. Verified twice over: byte-identical to 汽 qì, and also to the simplified 气, so the Canon's traditional graph is handled with no risk of the voice stumbling on it.
10.compromise: The initial is young. Middle Chinese had an aspirated velar (roughly khjɨjH) — the reason the Wade-Giles spelling is ch'i and the older English borrowing is 'chi' — and the modern [tɕʰ] is the eighteenth-century palatalisation again. Cantonese hei3 does not preserve the velar either; it lenited it to [h]. So for this word, one of the most-used in the whole tradition, neither living reading keeps the ancient consonant, and that is worth saying plainly. The alchemical variant 炁 is a different graph and is not what is spoken here.

11.why: The bare traditional character, verified byte-identical both to 音 yīn and to the simplified 阴 — so the traditional graph the Canon prints reaches the same correct reading.
11.compromise: Mandarin has lost the final consonant of this word. Middle Chinese 陰 ended in -m (roughly 'im), and the Ming merger of -m into -n means the modern yīn is homophonous with syllables that were never like it. Cantonese jam1 still ends in -m. Since 陰 and 陽 are the tradition's defining pair, it is worth knowing that in the language of the Xìcí they did not rhyme or end as they do now.

12.why: The bare traditional character, verified byte-identical to 羊 yáng and to the simplified 阳.
12.compromise: More conservative than its partner: the final -ŋ is genuinely old and survives in both modern readings, and the initial glide is a reasonable reflex of the Middle Chinese initial. What has moved is the tone system — the rising second tone here is the modern reflex of a Middle Chinese level tone in the lower register, a category that existed because the initial was voiced. So even where the segments hold, the melody is a modern reorganisation, and Old Chinese is thought to have had no tonal melody to reorganise.

13.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 午 wǔ. Rate 140 so the third-tone dip is fully realised rather than clipped.
13.compromise: Mandarin has deleted the initial consonant of this word altogether. Middle Chinese 五 began with [ŋ] (roughly nguX), which is why the Cantonese is ng5 — a syllable consisting of nothing but a syllabic nasal. Mandarin lost initial ŋ- entirely, leaving a bare vowel. This is the largest single segmental gap between the two buttons anywhere in the hall, and 五行 is the phrase it sits in.

14.why: A genuine polyphone and the first thing tested in this hall. Isolated 行 is byte-identical to 形, 型 and 刑 — xíng, second tone, which is the reading 五行 needs — and demonstrably NOT identical to 航 or 杭 (háng), the 'row, business' reading. The engine takes the right branch unaided; no forcing was needed.
14.compromise: The initial is modern. Middle Chinese had a voiced velar fricative here (the 匣 initial, roughly haeng), and Cantonese hang4 still has [h]; the Mandarin [ɕ] is the same eighteenth-century palatalisation that reshaped 巽, 氣 and 仙. The word the hall glosses as 'five phases' or 'five goings' is therefore pronounced today with a consonant the Warring States did not have. Note also that both modern readings, xíng and háng, descend from a split that was already present in Middle Chinese.

15.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 今 jīn — same syllable, same high level tone.
15.compromise: The best demonstration in the hall of how far Mandarin has travelled, because this one syllable lost BOTH ends. Middle Chinese 金 was roughly kim: a plain velar stop at the front and an -m at the back. Mandarin palatalised the velar to [tɕ] and merged the -m into -n, so not a single consonant of the modern jīn is the ancient one. Cantonese gam1 keeps both. Click the two buttons back to back on this character if you click them anywhere.

16.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 目 mù.
16.compromise: Another entering-tone casualty. Middle Chinese 木 ended in -k (roughly muwk); Mandarin has deleted the stop and redistributed the syllable into the fourth tone, so the modern mù is an open syllable where the ancient one was closed. Cantonese muk6 still has the [k̚]. The phase of the east is thus a shorter word in Beijing than it was in Chang'an, by one whole consonant.

17.why: The bare character. A monophone with one reading, read as an ordinary word; rate 140 for the third-tone dip.
17.compromise: Honestly flagged: this is one of the five readings that could not be homophone-verified, because Mandarin shuǐ has no second common character to test it against — 誰 is tone 2 in its literary reading and was confirmed different. The reading is not in doubt in any dictionary, but the check that validated the other thirty-six was unavailable here. Chronologically, the retroflex [ʂ] is a northern development from a Middle Chinese palatal (roughly syijX), and the rime has moved considerably; 上善若水 in the Dàodé jīng rhymed in a system this reading cannot show.

18.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 伙 huǒ. Rate 140 for the dip.
18.compromise: The Mandarin initial [x] is a fair continuation of the Middle Chinese voiceless fricative here (roughly xwaX), so this one is comparatively conservative in its consonant. The rime and the tone are modern. Note that the Cantonese fo2 is NOT more ancient here: Cantonese turned the fricative into [f] before rounded vowels, an innovation of its own, so on this character the second button is further from Middle Chinese than the first — an honest exception to the general pattern of this hall.

19.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 吐 tǔ — a useful check, since 吐 is itself a polyphone and its agreement here confirms the engine took the third-tone branch for both.
19.compromise: Segmentally among the closest to Middle Chinese in the hall: the aspirated dental stop survived, as did the back vowel (roughly thuX). What has changed is the tone system around it. The mediating phase of the centre is therefore one of the few signs here where a Tang reader would probably recognise the Mandarin word — which is the exception that makes the rest of the set worth hearing.

20.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 耽 dān.
20.compromise: Conservative in its segments — the dental stop and the final -n both descend directly from Middle Chinese tan — and modern only in its tone contour. This single character carries 內丹, 外丹, 金丹 and 丹田, so it is worth noting that here, unusually, the modern sound is close to the medieval one; the distance in this hall is not uniform, and pretending otherwise would be as false as pretending there is none.

21.why: The bare character, read as an ordinary word with the correct rising second tone.
21.compromise: One of the five unverified readings, and the reason is worth stating: Mandarin shén has no second common character to test against. 什 was tried and is read shí in isolation (byte-identical to 十), so it proved nothing; the contextual probe 神麼 against 什麼 was inconclusive, since one is a lexical entry and the other a nonce string. The reading is a monophone and not in doubt, but it escaped the test. Chronologically: Middle Chinese had a voiced palatal fricative initial here (roughly zyin); Mandarin devoiced it and retroflexed it, and the second tone is the reflex of that lost voicing. Cantonese san4 carries the same history in its tone register without the retroflexion.

22.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 京 jīng — the same syllable and the same high level tone.
22.compromise: The initial is the palatalisation again, from a Middle Chinese dental affricate (roughly tsjeng); Cantonese zing1 keeps an unpalatalised affricate. The final -ŋ is old and survives. So the first of the three treasures 精氣神 is spoken today with a consonant that postdates the entire alchemical literature that names it — as are the other two, which is a coincidence worth noticing when the three are clicked in order.

23.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 餛 hún — a rare partner deliberately chosen because it has only one reading.
23.compromise: The initial fricative and the final -n are both reasonable continuations of Middle Chinese hwon, so the segments are moderately conservative; the second tone is the modern reflex of a lower-register level tone. Cantonese wan4 has dropped the initial entirely, so on this character Mandarin is the more conservative button — again, the distance is not uniform. What neither shows is the Old Chinese form in which 魂 and 云 were phonetically related, which is why the graph is built the way it is.

24.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 破 pò.
24.compromise: Another entering-tone loss. Middle Chinese 魄 ended in -k (roughly phaek) and Mandarin has deleted it, leaving an open syllable in the fourth tone. Cantonese paak3 keeps the [k̚] and a much more open vowel. Worth hearing against 魂 immediately before it: the two-soul pair is a rhyming and structural unit in the sources, and in Mandarin the pair has lost the shape it had. 載營魄抱一 in Dàodé jīng 10 is Warring States verse and does not scan in either modern reading.

25.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 扶 fú.
25.compromise: The [f] is not ancient in either modern reading. Middle Chinese had a voiced bilabial here (roughly bju), and the shift of bilabials to labiodentals before certain rimes is a Tang-era change that Cantonese underwent as well — fu4 there, fú here. So on the talisman-character both buttons agree and both are post-Tang, which is the honest report: this is a place where the second system buys nothing. The rising tone is the reflex of the lost voicing.

26.why: A genuinely rare character and a real risk that the voice would not have it, so it was checked carefully: 籙 is byte-identical to 路 lù, and also to the simplified 箓, so Ting-Ting has the correct reading for the traditional graph the Canon prints.
26.compromise: Entering tone again: Middle Chinese 籙 ended in -k (roughly ljowk), Mandarin has deleted the stop, and Cantonese luk6 retains it. This is the ordination register — the document that defines what a priest may command — and its name in Mandarin is a syllable shorter at the end than the one written in the Tang manuals.

27.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 擂 léi.
27.compromise: Comparatively conservative in its consonant — the lateral is old (Middle Chinese roughly lwoj) — with a modernised rime and tone. Cantonese leoi4 shows a different rime development from the same source, so the two buttons here diverge without either being the ancestor. The 雷法 thunder rites are a twelfth-century development, which makes this one of the few items in the hall whose ritual context is closer in date to the modern readings than to Old Chinese.

28.why: A polyphone worth checking, and Mandarin behaves: isolated 易 is byte-identical to 意 yì, the correct fourth-tone reading, and the same syllable serves both the 'change' and the 'ease' senses in Mandarin, so no forcing is needed.
28.compromise: Mandarin has collapsed a distinction that Middle Chinese made and Cantonese still makes. The 'change' reading was an entering-tone syllable ending in -k (roughly yek); the 'ease' reading was not. Mandarin lost the final stops, and the two readings fell together as one yì — so the double sense the hall's note describes, change and ease in one graph, is genuinely inaudible in the default clip. Cantonese keeps them apart as jik6 against ji6, which is exactly why the second button exists. This is the clearest case in the hall where the modern reading destroys information the text depends on.

29.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 掛 guà.
29.compromise: The velar survived Mandarin's palatalisation because the rime is back rather than front — the same accident that spared 坤 and 金's Cantonese cousin — so the initial is old (Middle Chinese roughly kweaH). The rime and the tone are modern. As with 艮, the fourth tone reflects a Middle Chinese tone category, not a recoverable ancient pitch.

30.why: A rare character; verified byte-identical to 搖 yáo, which confirms both the syllable and the rising tone.
30.compromise: Mandarin has deleted the initial consonant. Middle Chinese 爻 began with [ŋ] (roughly ngaew) — Cantonese ngaau4 still shows it — and Mandarin's loss of initial ŋ- has left a bare glide. This is the second of the hall's two ŋ- words, with 五, and the pair are the best evidence in the set that the default clip is a modern language reading an ancient text rather than the text speaking. The 爻辭 line-statements are among the oldest layers of the Yìjīng.

31.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 添 tiān — the same syllable and the same high level tone.
31.compromise: Segmentally conservative: the aspirated dental and the final -n both come straight from Middle Chinese then, and the medial glide is old too. This is one of the handful of signs where the Mandarin reading would have been broadly intelligible to a Tang reader. The tone is a modern contour realising an inherited category, and the Old Chinese form — which is what 天 is in the Odes and in the Zhou bronze inscriptions — is further off than either.

32.why: Worth checking, because 地 has a neutral-tone use as a suffix. Isolated 地 is byte-identical to 弟 dì and demonstrably NOT identical to 的, so the engine gives the full fourth-tone reading and not the reduced particle.
32.compromise: Middle Chinese had a voiced initial here (roughly dijH); Mandarin devoiced it, and the fourth tone you hear is the trace that voicing left behind. Cantonese dei6 carries the same fact in its lower tone register. So the [t] is a devoicing rather than an inheritance. With 天 and 人 this makes the 三才, and the three are worth clicking in sequence: 天 is conservative, 地 is a devoicing, and the scheme they belong to is older than both readings.

33.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 先 xiān.
33.compromise: The initial is young, by the same palatalisation that reshaped 巽: Middle Chinese had a plain [s] (roughly sjen) and Cantonese sin1 still does. The transcendent's name in Beijing therefore begins with a consonant no Tang hagiographer used. The final -n is old. The older graph 僊 is a different character and is not what is spoken here.

34.why: The hall deliberately prints the Canon's variant graph 眞 (U+771E) rather than the standard 真, so the real question was whether the voice has it at all. It does, and correctly: 眞 is byte-identical to 真 and to 針 zhēn. The Canon's orthography costs nothing in the audio.
34.compromise: The retroflex is a Mandarin innovation from a Middle Chinese palatal (roughly tsyin); Cantonese zan1 has no retroflexion. The -n is old, the first tone is a modern contour on an inherited category. Note that what you hear is identical to a reading of 真: the variant is graphic only, and no pronunciation distinguishes 眞人 in the Canon from 真人 in a modern edition.

35.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 懸 xuán — same syllable, same rising tone, same front rounded medial.
35.compromise: Middle Chinese had a voiced velar fricative here (the 匣 initial, roughly hwen). Mandarin palatalised it to [ɕ]; Cantonese went the other way and lost the initial altogether, giving jyun4. So on 玄 — 玄之又玄, the gate of all wonders — neither living reading preserves the ancient consonant, and the two moderns have diverged in opposite directions from it. That is the honest position and it is more interesting than a clean story. The imperial name-taboos of 1012 and of the Kangxi reign affected the graph, not the sound.

36.why: The bare traditional character, verified byte-identical to 吳 wú and to the simplified 无 — so the traditional graph reaches the same reading, and the ancient variant 无 the hall's note mentions would sound identical anyway.
36.compromise: Mandarin has deleted the initial consonant. Middle Chinese 無 began with [m] (roughly mju), which Cantonese mou4 still has; Mandarin lost it through the same labial weakening that produced modern wú. So the word for absence has itself lost a segment, which is a coincidence the tradition would enjoy but which is a genuine sound change. 天下萬物生於有，有生於無 is Warring States verse and its shape depends on sounds neither button gives.

37.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 新 xīn.
37.compromise: Like 金, this syllable lost both ends. Middle Chinese 心 was roughly sim: a plain [s] and a final -m. Mandarin palatalised the [s] to [ɕ] in the eighteenth century and merged the -m into -n in the Ming, so neither consonant of the modern xīn is the ancient one. Cantonese sam1 keeps both. The Zhuāngzǐ's 心齋, the fasting of the heart-mind, is named with a word whose modern Beijing sound shares no consonant with the one Zhuangzi's readers used.

38.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 衣 yī. Because the clip is a single isolated syllable, what you get is the citation tone — first tone — and not one of the sandhi forms (yí, yì) that 一 takes before other syllables in running speech. For a letter-name click that is the right choice.
38.compromise: Mandarin has deleted this word's final consonant. Middle Chinese 一 ended in -t (roughly 'jit), an entering-tone syllable; Cantonese jat1 still ends in [t̚], and it is the only final -t anywhere in this hall. Mandarin's yī is an open syllable and shows nothing of it. Given how much weight the tradition puts on this graph — 守一, 抱一, the roll-call of chapter 39 — it is worth knowing that its modern name is a phonologically different word from the one those phrases were coined with.

39.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 態 tài.
39.compromise: Conservative in its initial: the aspirated dental descends directly from Middle Chinese (roughly thajH), and Cantonese taai3 agrees, so both buttons keep the consonant. The rime and the tone are modern. This character heads 太上老君, 太一, 太清 and 太極, and in those titles it is among the least-changed syllables the tradition uses — which makes the changed ones around it easier to hear.

cantonese.note: How the same characters are read in Hong Kong and Guangdong, where the Canon is also chanted — a living language, and on several points measurably closer to Middle Chinese than Mandarin is.

0.why: Forced, exactly as in Mandarin and for the same reason. `say -v Sin-ji "乾"` is byte-identical to 干 gon1 — the 'dry' reading, wrong for the Heaven trigram — and context does not help: 乾坤 differs from 虔坤 and 乾隆 differs from 虔隆, so Sin-ji has no kin4 reading of this graph anywhere. The substitute 虔 was verified byte-identical to 掮, a second independent kin4 character, and distinct from the voice's default 乾. The output is the kin4 syllable.
0.compromise: The audio comes from a different graph than the page shows; the waveform is nonetheless exactly what a correct 乾 would produce, since this engine synthesises from syllable and tone alone. Two-way corroboration only — 虔 and 掮 — where the Mandarin substitution had four, so this is the less-attested of the two forced clips. Chronologically, kin4 keeps the Middle Chinese velar initial that Mandarin palatalised away, and the lower-register tone 4 registers the fact that the initial was voiced in Middle Chinese. But Cantonese has devoiced it too: you hear [kʰ], not the voiced [g] of the Qieyun. Closer, not ancient.

1.why: The bare character. It is included as-is rather than substituted, and the reason is set out in the compromise — this is the weakest recipe in either system and the only one where a known error is being shipped deliberately.
1.compromise: THE TONE IS WRONG relative to the dictionary reading. Isolated 兌 in Sin-ji is byte-identical to 對 deoi3, the upper departing tone, where the standard Cantonese reading of this trigram is deoi6, the lower departing tone. In a tonal language that is not a shade of colour; it is a different word's melody. Two things keep it honest rather than fixable. First, deoi3 is not an invention: 兌換 is very commonly said deoi3 wun6 in Hong Kong, so what you hear is a real living reading, just not the one the Yìjīng commentaries use. Second, the obvious repair is unsafe: the only common deoi6 character is 隊, which itself has a colloquial deoi2 alongside its deoi6, and there is no second deoi6 character to corroborate it against — substituting it could replace a tone-3 error with a tone-2 error, and I cannot hear which. The clip therefore misses, says so, and the system's whole point is undercut on this one sign: deoi6's lower register is precisely the trace of the Middle Chinese voiced initial (roughly dwajH) that Cantonese is being offered for, and this clip does not show it.

2.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 厘 lei4 — same syllable, same low falling tone 4.
2.compromise: Tone 4 is the lower register, which in Cantonese marks a Middle Chinese voiced initial; here the initial was a lateral, and both modern readings keep it, so this is a sign where the two buttons differ mainly in rime and melody rather than in substance. Cantonese is not Middle Chinese: it has had a thousand years of its own change since the Qieyun, has merged rimes of its own, and its modern Hong Kong form has further mergers on top. Closer on the codas is the claim; nothing more.

3.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 振 zan3.
3.compromise: No retroflexion — Cantonese never made the northern retroflex series, so zan3 is closer to the Middle Chinese palatal affricate than Mandarin's zhèn in manner, though it is not that affricate either: Cantonese merged the whole palatal and dental series into one [ts]. The final -n is old in both readings. Tone 3 is the upper departing register, an inherited category with a modern contour.

4.why: A rare character, checked rather than assumed: byte-identical to 信 seon3, which fixes both syllable and tone.
4.compromise: Here the second button earns itself. Cantonese keeps the plain [s] that Middle Chinese had (roughly swonH) where Mandarin has the palatalised [ɕ] of xùn — an eighteenth-century northern change Cantonese never underwent. So on this sign the Cantonese initial is the older one by some seven hundred years. The rime and the tone contour are Cantonese's own; the claim is about the consonant.

5.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 砍 ham2.
5.compromise: A split verdict, and both halves matter. The final -m is genuinely ancient — Middle Chinese 坎 ended in -m, Mandarin merged all -m into -n in the Ming, and Cantonese ham2 preserves it. But the INITIAL is a Cantonese innovation: Middle Chinese had an aspirated velar (roughly khomX) and Cantonese lenited it to [h], which is why 坎 is ham2 and not kam2. So on this character each modern reading keeps the end the other lost, and neither is the Qieyun form. The formula 取坎填離 depends on no sound at all, being a formula about figures.

6.why: A rare character; verified byte-identical to 靳 gan3.
6.compromise: Conservative on both consonants — the velar and the -n are inherited, as they are in Mandarin — so the two buttons are close here and the difference is chiefly vowel and tone contour. Tone 3 is the upper departing register. Nothing in either reading recovers the Old Chinese form behind 艮其背 in the fifty-second hexagram, which is roughly two and a half thousand years older than either.

7.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 昆 kwan1.
7.compromise: One of the signs where Mandarin and Cantonese agree closely and both are reasonably conservative: the aspirated velar survived in both, because the following vowel is back and so escaped the northern palatalisation. Tone 1 is the upper level register. The Mother of the eight is therefore among the least informative clips for hearing the difference between the two systems — worth saying, so that the pairs which do differ are not lost in a general impression that everything differs.

8.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 度 dou6 — the lower departing tone, which is the reading the Canon uses.
8.compromise: Tone 6 is doing historical work: the lower register is Cantonese's record of the Middle Chinese voiced initial (roughly dawX), which Cantonese, like Mandarin, has itself devoiced — so the [t] you hear is not the ancient [d], only its tonal shadow. This is the general shape of the Cantonese claim throughout: the tone system remembers distinctions the consonants no longer make. Neither reading is the sound of 道可道，非常道, and the Odes-era rhymes that the Warring States corpus draws on work in neither.

9.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 得 dak1 — a partner that is a polyphone in Mandarin but not in Cantonese, which is exactly why it works here.
9.compromise: The flagship of the second system. Middle Chinese 德 ended in -k (roughly tok), and Cantonese keeps that final stop, unreleased, as [k̚]; Mandarin dé has deleted it entirely along with the whole entering-tone category. Play the two buttons in succession on this character and the loss is audible in under two seconds. Two honest qualifications: the Cantonese entering tone is a modern reflex, and its vowel has shifted from the Middle Chinese one; and Cantonese has merged the Middle Chinese three-way entering-tone register into its own scheme. It keeps the coda, not the syllable.

10.why: The bare traditional character, verified byte-identical to 器 hei3.
10.compromise: Cantonese is NOT closer here, and the page should not imply that it always is. Middle Chinese had an aspirated velar (roughly khjɨjH); Mandarin palatalised it to [tɕʰ], Cantonese lenited it to [h], and neither kept the velar stop. So for the single most-used word in the whole tradition both living readings have moved, in different directions, and the Wade-Giles 'ch'i' preserves a memory of the velar that neither button supplies. Tone 3 is the upper departing register.

11.why: The bare traditional character, verified byte-identical to 音 jam1.
11.compromise: The final -m is the point: Middle Chinese 陰 ended in -m, Mandarin merged it into -n during the Ming, and Cantonese keeps it. Since 陰 and 陽 are the tradition's defining pair, this is one of the clearest places to hear that the Xìcí's 一陰一陽之謂道 had a shape the default reading does not give. Qualification: modern Hong Kong Cantonese is stable on final -m, so this feature is safe, but the vowel and the tone contour are Cantonese's own and not medieval.

12.why: The bare traditional character, verified byte-identical to 羊 joeng4.
12.compromise: The final -ŋ is old in both readings, so this half of the pair is not where the systems diverge — 陰 is. What Cantonese adds here is the lower tone register, tone 4, marking the Middle Chinese voiced initial. The rounded front vowel [œː] is a distinctively Cantonese development and is not ancient. Clicking 陰 then 陽 in Cantonese gives the pair with its Middle Chinese codas intact; clicking them in Mandarin gives it with one of them gone.

13.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 伍 ng5. A syllable made of nothing but a syllabic nasal, which is the striking thing about it.
13.compromise: Marked medium for a specific and unverifiable reason. The whole interest of this clip is the initial [ŋ], which Mandarin has deleted and which descends from the Middle Chinese initial (roughly nguX) — but modern Hong Kong Cantonese has a widespread 'lazy sound' (懶音) tendency to drop initial ŋ-, and I cannot hear whether Sin-ji has it. If she does, this syllable arrives as a bare vowel and the clip demonstrates nothing at all. The homophone test cannot detect this, because 五 and 伍 would merge identically either way. Treat the [ŋ] as claimed rather than confirmed. Tone 5 is the lower rising register.

14.why: A polyphone in Cantonese too, and it was checked: isolated 行 is byte-identical to 恆 and 衡 (hang4, the 'go' reading, which is what 五行 needs) and demonstrably NOT identical to 航 (hong4, the 'row' reading). The engine takes the right branch unaided.
14.compromise: Cantonese keeps the Middle Chinese [h] initial (the 匣 series, roughly haeng) where Mandarin has the palatalised [ɕ] of xíng — so on this sign the second button is the older one by several centuries. The final -ŋ is old in both. Note that Cantonese also has a colloquial haang4 for 行 'to walk'; the literary hang4 you hear is the right register for a classical text and is what the engine gave. Tone 4 is the lower level register, marking the Middle Chinese voiced initial that Cantonese has itself devoiced to plain [h].

15.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 今 gam1.
15.compromise: The single best demonstration in this hall, and the one to send a reader to first. Middle Chinese 金 was roughly kim — velar stop, final -m — and Cantonese gam1 keeps both, where Mandarin jīn has palatalised the one and merged away the other, so not a consonant survives in the default reading. Two caveats that keep it honest: the vowel is Cantonese's own and is not the Middle Chinese one, and tone 1 is a modern contour on an inherited category. The claim is about the two consonants, and on those it is exact.

16.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 目 muk6.
16.compromise: Entering tone preserved: Middle Chinese 木 ended in -k (roughly muwk) and Cantonese keeps the unreleased [k̚] that Mandarin has deleted. Tone 6 here is the lower entering register, which in Cantonese is a genuine descendant of the Middle Chinese 入聲 category — the categorical inheritance is real even though the pitch values are modern. The phase of the east is one syllable's worth of consonant longer in Canton than in Beijing, and that consonant is the ancient one.

17.why: The bare character, read as an ordinary word with the rising tone 2.
17.compromise: One of the five unverified readings in the two systems: Cantonese seoi2 has no second common character to test it against, so this clip did not get the homophone check that the other thirty-eight in this system passed. The reading is not in doubt in any dictionary. Segmentally, Cantonese has no retroflexion where Mandarin has [ʂ], which puts it nearer the Middle Chinese palatal (roughly syijX) in manner, but the [sɵy] rime is a Cantonese development and not a medieval one. 上善若水 rhymes in neither reading.

18.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 夥 fo2.
18.compromise: Cantonese is FURTHER from Middle Chinese here than Mandarin is, and that should be said outright. The Middle Chinese initial was a voiceless fricative, roughly xwaX; Mandarin's [x] continues it directly, while Cantonese turned the fricative into [f] before rounded vowels, an innovation of its own. So on the fire phase the second button is the younger one. The general claim of this system is about codas — -p, -t, -k, -m — not about initials, and on initials it loses about as often as it wins.

19.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 討 tou2.
19.compromise: Both readings keep the aspirated dental from Middle Chinese thuX, so the systems agree on the consonant and differ only in rime and tone contour — Cantonese has diphthongised the vowel where Mandarin kept it back and simple, and here Mandarin's rime is arguably the more conservative. Tone 2 is the upper rising register. A quiet clip, and useful precisely because it shows the two systems close together.

20.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 單 daan1 — a partner deliberately chosen and confirmed, since 單 has other readings in personal names.
20.compromise: Close to Mandarin and close to Middle Chinese tan on both consonants; the audible difference between the buttons is the long [aː] against Mandarin's shorter vowel, and Cantonese's phonemic vowel length is a Cantonese development, not an inheritance. The whole alchemical vocabulary — 內丹, 外丹, 金丹, 丹田 — hangs on this one graph, and it is among the signs where the two thousand years have cost least.

21.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 臣 san4 — which is worth noting, because the equivalent Mandarin check had no available partner and 神 is the one reading confirmed on this side and not the other.
21.compromise: Middle Chinese had a voiced palatal fricative (roughly zyin). Cantonese devoiced it to plain [s] and recorded the voicing in the lower tone register, tone 4; Mandarin devoiced it and retroflexed it. Neither keeps the ancient consonant, and Cantonese's [s] is the product of a merger that flattened the whole palatal series. What survives on this side is the final -n and the tone category. 精氣神 as a set can be clicked through in either system; in neither does it sound as it did to Ge Hong.

22.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 晶 zing1.
22.compromise: Cantonese keeps an unpalatalised affricate where Mandarin has [tɕ], so the initial is closer to Middle Chinese tsjeng — but only closer, since Cantonese has merged the Middle Chinese dental and palatal affricate series into a single [ts]. The final -ŋ is old in both. First of the three treasures, and the one where the second button's advantage is real but modest.

23.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 云 wan4 — which is neat, since 云 is the phonetic element in the graph itself.
23.compromise: Cantonese has dropped the initial consonant here. Middle Chinese 魂 began with a fricative (roughly hwon) and Mandarin's [x] continues it; Cantonese wan4 has lost it, so on this character Mandarin is the more conservative button. The final -n and the lower tone register are inherited on this side. The homophony with 云 in Cantonese is a modern accident, not evidence about the graph's construction, which reflects a much older sound relationship.

24.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 拍 paak3.
24.compromise: Entering tone preserved: Middle Chinese 魄 ended in -k (roughly phaek), Cantonese keeps the unreleased [k̚] and the open [aː], and Mandarin's pò has neither. Click 魂 then 魄 on this side and then the same pair on the Mandarin side: the two-soul pair has a shape here that the default reading has flattened. Caveat as always — the [k̚] is a real inherited coda, but the vowel length and the tone-3 pitch are modern Cantonese.

25.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 扶 fu4.
25.compromise: Both systems agree and both are post-Tang. Middle Chinese had a voiced bilabial (roughly bju), and the shift of bilabials to labiodentals happened in the ancestry of Cantonese as well as of Mandarin, so fu4 and fú are equally young in their initial. Cantonese adds only the lower tone register as a record of the lost voicing. On the talisman-character the second button buys nothing, and pretending otherwise would misrepresent what this system is for.

26.why: A rare character with a real risk of not being in the voice's lexicon, so it was checked twice: byte-identical to 六 luk6 and to 錄 luk6. Sin-ji has it, and correctly.
26.compromise: Entering tone preserved: Middle Chinese 籙 ended in -k (roughly ljowk) and Cantonese keeps it where Mandarin's lù does not. This matters more here than the general case, because 籙 is a technical term of ordination conferred at Longhu Shan today and read aloud in Cantonese liturgy in Hong Kong — so the older-sounding reading is also a currently used one, not an antiquarian exercise. Tone 6 is the lower entering register.

27.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 擂 leoi4.
27.compromise: The lateral initial is inherited in both readings; the two systems have taken the Middle Chinese rime (roughly lwoj) in different directions, and neither [lɵy] nor Mandarin's [lei̯] is the ancestor. Tone 4 is the lower level register. The 雷法 thunder rites are twelfth-century, which puts them nearer these readings than most of the hall's material, though still several centuries adrift of both.

28.why: Forced, and the most valuable forcing in the set. Isolated 易 in Sin-ji is byte-identical to 二 and 義 — ji6, the 'easy' reading — which would name the Yìjīng the Book of Ease. The substitute 亦 was verified three ways, byte-identical to 譯, 液 and 疫, all jik6, so the output is the 'change' reading with its final stop. Sin-ji does know the right reading in one lexical context — 周易 is byte-identical to 周亦 — but not in 易經 and not in isolation, so the substitution is necessary.
28.compromise: The audio is generated from a different graph than the page shows, though the waveform is exactly what a correct jik6 reading of 易 would give. What this clip buys is worth the substitution: Middle Chinese distinguished the 'change' reading, an entering-tone syllable ending in -k (roughly yek), from the 'ease' reading, which was not. Mandarin lost the final stops and collapsed them into a single yì; Cantonese still keeps them apart as jik6 against ji6. So the hall's note that the same graph carries change and ease in 'another reading' is audible here and inaudible in the default system. The [k̚] is inherited; the vowel and pitch are modern Cantonese.

29.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 掛 gwaa3.
29.compromise: Both systems keep the Middle Chinese velar (roughly kweaH), since the back rime spared it from Mandarin's palatalisation, so the buttons agree on the consonant and differ in rime and contour. Tone 3 is the upper departing register. A sign where the second system adds little, listed as such.

30.why: A rare character; verified byte-identical to 肴 ngaau4.
30.compromise: Marked medium for the same unverifiable reason as 五. The interest of the clip is the initial [ŋ], inherited from Middle Chinese ngaew and deleted entirely in Mandarin — but modern Hong Kong Cantonese widely drops initial ŋ-, and the homophone test cannot detect whether Sin-ji does, since 爻 and 肴 would merge identically with or without it. If the ŋ- is absent you hear a bare glide and the clip demonstrates nothing. Claimed, not confirmed. Tone 4 is the lower level register; the diphthong is Cantonese's own.

31.why: The bare character, read as an ordinary word.
31.compromise: Unverified, and honestly so: Cantonese tin1 has no second common character to test against — 添, the obvious candidate, turns out to be tim1 in Cantonese and was confirmed different, which is a fact about the ref and not about 天 — and 田 tin4 was confirmed different, as its tone requires. So this reading, alone in the Cantonese set apart from 水, rests on the dictionary rather than on the test. 天 is a monophone and the risk is small. Segmentally it is conservative on both sides: the aspirated dental and the -n come straight from Middle Chinese then, and Mandarin agrees. This is a sign where the systems converge.

32.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 哋 dei6 — an unusual partner (the Cantonese plural marker) chosen precisely because it is unambiguous in this rime and tone.
32.compromise: Tone 6, the lower departing register, is Cantonese's record of the Middle Chinese voiced initial (roughly dijH), which Cantonese has itself devoiced — so the [t] is not ancient, only its tonal shadow is. Mandarin encodes the same history as its fourth tone. Neither reading recovers the initial. With 天 and 人 this makes the 三才; in this system the three are unusually close to Mandarin, and the pairs worth hearing are elsewhere.

33.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 先 sin1.
33.compromise: Cantonese keeps the plain [s] of Middle Chinese sjen where Mandarin has the palatalised [ɕ] of xiān, so on this sign the second button preserves a consonant Mandarin lost around the eighteenth century — the same win as at 巽 and 心. The final -n is old in both. Qualification: the [iː] and the tone-1 contour are Cantonese's own. The older graph 僊 is a different character and is not spoken here.

34.why: The Canon's variant graph 眞 (U+771E) rather than the standard 真, so the coverage question had to be settled: it was, byte-identical to 真 in Sin-ji as in Ting-Ting. The Canon's orthography costs nothing in either system.
34.compromise: No retroflexion, so the initial is nearer Middle Chinese tsyin in manner than Mandarin's zhēn — but Cantonese reached its [ts] by merging the palatal and dental series wholesale, so it is a different consonant from the medieval one and merely happens to be less distant. The -n is old, tone 1 is the upper level register. What you hear is identical to a reading of 真: the variant is graphic only, and 眞人, 眞武 and Quánzhēn sound the same whichever graph is printed.

35.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 元 jyun4 — the same syllable, the same low tone 4.
35.compromise: Cantonese has lost the initial consonant here altogether. Middle Chinese had a voiced velar fricative (the 匣 initial, roughly hwen); Mandarin palatalised it to [ɕ], Cantonese deleted it, and the modern jyun4 begins with nothing but a glide. So on 玄 — 玄之又玄，眾妙之門 — the second button is the further of the two from Middle Chinese, and the honest report is that the two living readings have diverged in opposite directions from a consonant neither now has. Tone 4 marks the lost voicing. The name-taboos of 1012 and of the Kangxi reign affected the graph, not the sound.

36.why: The bare traditional character, verified byte-identical to 毛 mou4.
36.compromise: Cantonese keeps the initial [m] of Middle Chinese mju, which Mandarin deleted on its way to wú — so on the word for absence the second button has a consonant the first has lost. The rime [ou̯] is a Cantonese development, and tone 4 is the lower level register marking the historically voiced initial. Note that the ancient variant 无 the hall mentions is a graphic matter and would sound the same. 天下萬物生於有，有生於無 is Warring States verse whose shape neither reading gives.

37.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 深 sam1.
37.compromise: With 金, the pair to click if a reader clicks only two. Middle Chinese 心 was roughly sim — a plain [s] and a final -m — and Cantonese sam1 keeps both, where Mandarin's xīn palatalised the one and merged away the other, leaving no ancient consonant standing. The Zhuāngzǐ's 心齋 is named with a word whose Cantonese form still has the shape it had in the Qieyun, at least at both ends. The vowel and the tone contour are modern; the claim is about the consonants and on those it is exact.

38.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 壹 jat1, the formal numeral — an unambiguous partner. Cantonese has no tone sandhi on 一 of the kind Mandarin applies, so the isolated clip is also the running form.
38.compromise: The only final -t anywhere in this hall. Middle Chinese 一 ended in -t (roughly 'jit) and Cantonese keeps it as an unreleased [t̚], while Mandarin's yī is an open syllable that shows nothing of it. Given how much the tradition rests on this graph — 守一, 抱一, the chapter 39 roll-call of what obtained the One — it is the clearest single case for offering this system at all. The [t̚] is a real inherited coda; the vowel and the tone-1 pitch are modern Cantonese, and Cantonese's entering tones are a reorganised descendant of the Middle Chinese category rather than that category itself.

39.why: The bare character, verified byte-identical to 泰 taai3.
39.compromise: Both systems keep the aspirated dental of Middle Chinese thajH, so the initial is inherited on both sides and the buttons differ chiefly in vowel length and tone contour, neither of which is ancient. This character heads 太上老君, 太一, 太清 and 太極; it is among the least-changed syllables in the hall, and that is worth saying at the end of a set whose whole point has been how much has changed elsewhere.
